turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Hi, Dr. Smith. Well, I'm here because... I just can't stop focusing on my face. There's this droop and unevenness around my mouth and my jaw, and I see it in every single reflection or photo. People keep telling me I look fine, but it just feels so obvious to me. It's gotten to the point where it's really affecting my work—I've actually started avoiding client meetings and presentations because I just don't want anyone looking at it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes an intense preoccupation with a perceived droop and unevenness in their face that others say looks fine.
symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient mentions constantly seeing the perceived defect in reflections and photos, and avoiding client meetings and presentations because of it.

turns.doctor_question: When you avoid these meetings, is it primarily because you feel your appearance is flawed, or are you worried that others will judge, criticize, or mock your appearance?
turns.patient_response: I'm not really sure. I guess... I haven't really thought about it like that. I just know that I feel like it looks awful. I don't know if I'm expecting them to actually mock me or say anything out loud about it. I just... I just know I can't stand the thought of anyone looking at my face.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient states they feel their face looks awful and cannot stand the thought of anyone looking at it, indicating a preoccupation with a perceived flaw in their appearance.

turns.doctor_question: If you were in a situation where you knew for certain that no one would judge or criticize your appearance, would you still feel the urge to avoid being seen?
turns.patient_response: Yes, I think I would. Because, well, even right now when people tell me I look fine, it doesn't really change anything for me. I just can't stop seeing that droop and the unevenness around my jaw. Every time I catch a reflection or look at a photo, it's right there. It feels so obvious and terrible to me that I just... I can't face it. That's really why I've been avoiding my clients and stepping back from presentations at work. It's what I see that bothers me so much, even if I knew for a fact no one else was judging me for it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes an intense, persistent preoccupation with a perceived droop and unevenness around her jaw that others say looks fine, which drives her to avoid being seen.

turns.doctor_question: How much time on an average day would you say you spend checking your reflection or examining the area around your mouth and jaw?
turns.patient_response:
Honestly, it's hours. Especially before work or if there's some kind of family event... I can spend hours just standing at the bathroom mirror. 

I'll take pictures on my phone from a bunch of different angles to check how the droop looks, and then I'll end up redoing my makeup or adjusting my scarf over and over to try and hide it. I'm constantly asking my husband if my face looks lopsided to him. And then... I usually end up scrolling through photos of other women on my phone, just comparing my face to theirs to see how bad mine looks beside them. So, on an average day, it takes up a really large amount of my time.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes a severe preoccupation with a perceived 'droop' or 'lopsided' appearance in her face, which consumes hours of her day.
symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient explicitly details repetitive behaviors in response to her appearance concerns, including mirror checking, taking photos, camouflaging with makeup and scarves, seeking reassurance from her husband, and comparing herself to other women.
